" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/076b4a1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5463x3066+0+288/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F14%2Fce%2Fa033aad94e37bdfadcdad57a5a95%2Fguns-020121-16.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5e6de6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5463x3066+0+288/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F14%2Fce%2Fa033aad94e37bdfadcdad57a5a95%2Fguns-020121-16.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/076b4a1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5463x3066+0+288/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F14%2Fce%2Fa033aad94e37bdfadcdad57a5a95%2Fguns-020121-16.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Jeff Regnier, owner of now-closed Kee Firearms & Training, at his New Lenox store in 2021. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Regnier said the legal battle prompted him to close his gun store and transfer his firearms inventory to his sister in Georgia, a sheriff’s deputy who is also a federally licensed firearms dealer.</p><p>“We still owe the IRS money,” Regnier said. “Mortgages. Attorneys. Workers. It’s been tough.”</p><p>“They have made life very difficult for us,” Keranen said.</p><p>The couple eventually recovered $4.4 million from frozen investment accounts but say Will County still owes them about $2 million in lost investment gains.</p><h3>More legal fights ahead</h3><p>The original criminal case tied to the pandemic loans is now on hold as a judge considers a request from the couple to appoint a special prosecutor to investigate Will County’s forfeiture unit and federal agents.</p><p>In a court filing, the couple's lawyer argues that the alleged abuses of the forfeiture system in the case were “neither isolated nor an aberration in Will County.”</p><p>Andreano said forfeiture laws allow government agencies to build “slush funds” with little oversight. </p><p>He also said prosecutors had a financial incentive in the couple's case: Any restitution ordered in the criminal case would go to the federal Small Business Administration, not to Will County.</p><p>“So they filed a forfeiture case to grab money for the county,” he said.</p><p>Andreano is challenging Illinois forfeiture laws in another case, this one involving an 85-year-old woman whose 2014 Mazda CX-5 was seized by New Lenox police after her daughter was stopped for an expired registration sticker.</p><p>Regnier, who ran unsuccessfully for Congress in a Republican primary in 2022, said the forfeiture system gives prosecutors enormous leverage.</p><p>“They hold you under water and say, ‘Let’s make a deal,’ ” he said.</p><p>Keranen said she witnessed the human toll of the system while in court.</p><p>“We saw people coming into the forfeiture court crying,” she said. “I think it needs reform. I’m not sure it needs to be abolished. But they shouldn’t be able to take your stuff without proving a crime.”</p>

entries.title: When freedom was fragile: How Quinn Chapel AME put its faith in action
entries.summary: <p>Black people in Antebellum America wrestled to secure and maintain their freedom as America’s original sin of slavery pulled at the seams of the tapestry of the Union.</p><p>In 1787, slavery was outlawed in the territory that would become Illinois. But, in 1819, a year after lawmakers created the state’s first constitution, they passed the first of several Black Laws that threw free Black people into a new form of bondage.</p><p>These laws, also known as the Black Codes, denied free Blacks basic civil rights that should be afforded to them as citizens. The laws also made Illinois an unwelcoming place for Black people to live. They couldn’t stay in the state for more than 10 days, unless they registered their freedom papers with the respective county clerk’s office. Only white children could access public school education. Black people were even forbidden from gathering in groups of three or more.</p><p>That is, unless it was for religious observances like church meetings.</p><p>By the 1840s, Chicago’s Black population inched towards 140 people as free Blacks flocked to the city to steer clear of slavery throughout the American South. Some of them started Quinn Chapel AME, the city’s first Black church.</p><p>The year was 1844. Rev. Abraham Hall started a prayer band with six members in the home of John Day, located near State and Lake streets. Two years later, the members made their first purchase, which became the city’s first Black-owned property for religious purposes. By 1847, the church became an official congregation within the African Methodist Episcopal church and was named after Bishop William Paul Quinn, who organized AME churches across the Midwest.</p><p>Beyond its physical building, the Black Church became the “locust of community activism,” according to Jennifer Harbour, associate professor of history at the University of Nebraska Omaha.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ac0000" name="module-ac0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items class="Figure-content"><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Eric White / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div></div> </div><p>The physical building of the church not only served as a beacon for freedom seekers, but it was also the place where free Blacks could develop. As the law closed them off from public society, the church became the center of the community. It was where people learned to read, engaged in debate club, had women’s Bible study, and singing classes.</p><p>“It is the place where people can feel safe, both spiritually and temporally. And it also is the place where Black abolitionism really has its start,” Harbour said. “I can't think of anything that's more important to the Black community than the church in this period.”</p><p>In its early years, Quinn Chapel stood as a community pillar where even the most affluent members organized their role in the emancipation movement, and today the church remains a relic of when the Christian faith fueled action toward Black liberation.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" It permitted slave catchers to travel across the country to recapture enslaved people who sought freedom.</p><p>In response, Quinn Chapel members held a special meeting to denounce the law and make it known where they stood on the issue. According to Quinn Chapel’s National Register of Historic Places <a class="Link" href="https://nara-media.s3.amazonaws.com/electronic-records/rg-079/NPS_IL/79000827.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>application</u></a>, the members are reported to have said, “We will stand by our liberty at the expense of our lives, and will not consent to be taken into slavery or permit our brethren to be taken.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-9e0000" name="html-embed-module-9e0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-map" data-src="visualisation/28031486"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/28031486/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="map visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Though Quinn Chapel members were free, they knew their freedom was precarious. Harbour said the Fugitive Slave Law strengthened Quinn Chapel members’ commitment to emancipation everywhere.</p><p>“African Americans are prescient enough at this stage to say ‘just because I’m not in the South now doesn’t mean I can’t be transported there overnight. Railroad. For those on foot to freedom, this location made continuing their journey to Canada easier.</p><p>Harbour said Christianity was a major fuel behind the power of the Underground Railroad.</p><p>“So the Underground Railroad is a very physical thing that helps people get from point A to point B,” Harbour said. “But when you talk about the maturation of social activism in the Black community, that it’s funneled through Christianity. It’s funneled through the church.”</p><p>The church made organizing collective efforts possible. Darling, photographer</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The women would consider questions like “Are we going to give money to the people coming through the Underground Railroad,” Harbour said. “It’s way more than just mules and men.”</p><p>At times, both the church building itself and the homes of some members, including The Big Four, doubled as refuges to conceal the enslaved. Freedom seekers were tucked away in a crawl space, with barely enough room to breathe, all to remain hidden from slave catchers.</p><p>The church’s activism also included direct protest of the Fugitive Slave Act by collaborating with the Liberty Association vigilance committee. The Liberty Association was an extension of the Liberty Party, a political party of the 1840s and 1850s designed to run candidates to end slavery through political action.</p><p>In Chicago, the association was a sort of Black police force “where people are going to go out and watch to see if there are slave catchers coming from the South,” Harbour said.</p><p>At the time, the Black Codes were still in effect, which made their emancipation tactics risky. There were severe consequences – through both local and federal laws — for violating the Fugitive Slave Act or helping to emancipate an enslaved person.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> </figure> </div> </div><p>Under the Illinois Black Codes, people could be fined $200, if they brought a freedom seeker to Illinois under the pretense of emancipating them. If they couldn’t pay the fines, they’d be forced to use their labor to pay off the debt owed, which was essentially slavery by another name. And if freedom seekers were caught more than 10 miles from the home of their owners, they’d face a penalty of up to 35 bare back lashings.</p><p>The veil of class, wealth, and mixed ancestry did not fool Quinn Chapel members into thinking they couldn’t be returned to slavery or taken into bondage for the first time. Harbour said this sober reality motivated them to defy the risks and to commit themselves to emancipation for all: “We got a nice house, and we've arrived, and we've built these beautiful churches. … But none of us have freedom until all of us have freedom.”</p><h3><b>Quinn Chapel Elite Lead the Way </b></h3><p>The free Black people who led Quinn Chapel’s emancipation work were among the city’s Black elite. They were leaders in the business community and politics. Key leading families were the Atkinsons and the Joneses.</p><p>Emma Atkinson and her husband, Isaac Atkinson, arrived in Chicago at some point between <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/curious-city/2023/02/24/oldest-families-in-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>1847</u></a> and 1853. They were born of free ancestry, which included Black, Scottish, and Cherokee Native American. Isaac started a transportation company that helped Black people travel along Chicago’s early roads by horse and mule. Emma rose in leadership as a key leader of Quinn Chapel’s “Big Four.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a citizens.</p><p>The patriarch, John Jones, was born free, in 1816, in North Carolina to a mixed-race mother and a father of German descent. Jones was regularly plagued by the fear of being enslaved. At an early age, his mother sent him to become an apprentice to a white man to keep him out of reach. Years later, when his father passed away, Jones was concerned that his white brothers might enslave him as part of their inheritance. Jones befriended a blacksmith of a socially ranked Black family. He joined that family on their voyage to Illinois. Jones was a tailor, businessman, philanthropist, Underground Railroad activist, abolitionist, civil rights activist, county commissioner and the first African American to hold elective office in Illinois.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Chicago History Museum</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The couple arrived in Chicago with $3.50 to their names. John taught himself how to read and slowly built a business as a tailor, leveraging the skills he’d learned from his father who was a master tailor. He used the wealth he accumulated not only to sustain his family but also to support people who made their way to Chicago via the Underground Railroad.</p><p>The Joneses’ home was located on Monroe and Dearborn, not far from where Quinn Chapel stood on Jackson and Dearborn. Both provided refuge to freedom seekers. Will Miller, Quinn Chapel’s historic preservation chair, said that as the homes doubled as stations, they made “sure that those people were housed and then got to the next location.”</p><p>In addition to aiding freedom seekers, John Jones also spoke out against the Black Codes. In 1864, he published a 16-page pamphlet called <i>The Black Laws of Illinois and a Few Reasons Why They Should Be Repealed. </i>Two years after the Emancipation Proclamation was signed, on February 7, 1865, the Illinois legislature rescinded the Black Laws.</p><p>Years later, in 1871, his activism propelled him toward a successful bid to become a Cook County Commissioner, making him the first There’s a massive organ that the church purchased from the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition German pavilion.The church members, ever focused on the church's financial wellbeing and future, held the first ever June Rose benefit concert to pay for the organ. While they’ve cleared the debt, they’ve hosted the concerts for more than 130 years. Venning said “It's kind of a homecoming for everybody.”</p><p>Above the organ is a mural that was unique for its time. Like many art pieces, Venning said this was a form of resistance.</p><p>“If you think about 1904 and what was happening in the country at that time, this was a direct slap in the face to what folks Dr. Martin Luther King Jr</u></a>, Susan B. Anthony, Frederick Douglass, and Ida B. Wells. They denounced hate and amplified messages of freedom and equality.</p><p>Venning said the fact that Quinn Chapel still stands today is a testament to faith and the power of the divine. Quinn Chapel was built on the edge of the historic Prairie District neighborhood, an area dubbed “Millionaire's Row” where Marshall Field and George Pullman once lived.</p><p>It was an area where residents likely “didn’t want Black folks nearby,” Venning said. “We’d like to say that the Holy Spirit inspired them to leave us alone because they heard it was going to be a church, and so they didn’t bother us.”</p><p>And 133 years later, that church is still standing.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0f0000" name="module-0f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>CHICAGO’S BLACK CHURCHES</h3><br>“Faith in Action” is an occasional series, from WBEZ and the Sun-Times, on the history and impact of the Black Church in Chicago. In addition to Quinn Chapel, the series will feature the history and work of several Black churches, including:<br><ul id="rte-4c0b4122-1e7c-11f1-a5cd-9195eabad01f"><li>Olivet Baptist Church</li><li>Vernon Park Church of God</li><li>Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church</li><li>Lawndale Christian Community Church</li><li>Progressive Baptist Church</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago police, other agencies take in millions by seizing cars, cash even without an arrest or conviction
entries.summary: <p>Courtroom 1707 at the Daley Center. People steadily stream in, hoping they'll end up able to hold onto what's often their most valuable possession: a car.</p><p>Most are Black or Latino. Most don’t have lawyers. And many are trying to stop the government from taking their vehicles for good.</p><p>Every year, the Chicago Police Department and other law enforcement agencies across Illinois seize thousands of cars, along with piles of cash and other property. Prosecutors say the seized assets are tied to crimes that range from drug offenses to traffic violations — and occasionally violent acts.</p><p>The seizures bring in millions of dollars for law enforcement.</p><p>But critics say the Illinois civil asset forfeiture system flips on its head a foundational rule of American justice: You're innocent until proven guilty.</p><p>Under Illinois law, though, the police can seize property based on suspicion alone — even if the owner is never arrested, never charged with any crime, never convicted.</p><p>A 2023 report from the Chicago Appleseed Center for Fair Courts, an advocacy group, called for Illinois to scrap civil asset forfeitures, arguing that the system is fundamentally unfair.</p><p>U.S. Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch has questioned the constitutionality of civil asset forfeiture, saying, "Even innocent owners can wait for months or years for forfeiture proceedings to play out.”</p><p>State lawmakers have passed modest reforms over the past decade, shifting the burden onto the government to prove that property seized is tied to crime and requiring agencies to provide some details on what they seize and how they spend it.</p><p>Supporters, though, say the system works and should be kept in place.</p><p>“I am 100% for this,” says Tom Weitzel, retired chief of the Riverside police department. “Activists are taking a handful of cases and exploiting them for political gain as if they represent the whole system. They don’t.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-dd0000" name="image-dd0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Tom Weitzel, former chief of the Riverside police department.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Inside ‘forfeiture court’</b></h3><p>To get a closeup look at how the system works, we went to the Daley Center, where Courtroom 1707 is Ground Zero for forfeitures in Cook County.</p><p>On Mondays and Wednesdays, dozens of people — most of them appearing on screen via Zoom — respond to lawsuits filed by prosecutors seeking to keep their property. Tuesdays and Thursdays, the trials that stem from these cases are held.</p><p>There are a lot of them. Last year, more than 3,100 forfeiture cases were filed in Cook County.</p><p>In court, the judges walk people through the maze of legal steps. You file a claim, enter an appearance, submit an answer.</p><p>For those without lawyers, though, the paperwork can be overwhelming.</p><p>Supporters of a bill being considered in Springfield say they're aiming to streamline the system by allowing prosecutors to send forfeiture notices by email instead of regular mail.</p><p>Some defense lawyers say they worry that those emailed notices could wind up buried in spam folders.</p><p>Missing one can be devastating. If people fail to respond within 45 days, a judge can order their property forfeited by default.</p><p>Even people who don’t technically own their cars — they bought them but are still paying off their car loans — can see their credit take a big hit if a vehicle is taken.</p><p>Sometimes, judges return cars temporarily when the owners argue that a seizure is causing hardship because they can’t get to work or school.</p><p>Others file what’s known as an “innocent owner” defense, claiming that someone else — often a relative — was driving their vehicle.</p><p>For many people navigating the system alone, it’s a lot to absorb and often confusing.</p><h3><b>Waiting a year for $5,000</b></h3><p>Two men appeared in court recently trying to recover about $5,000 each that Chicago police officers took from them after a traffic stop in which officers found a small amount of cannabis. The men say they’re auto dealers and were carrying the cash to buy a vehicle. They told a judge the misdemeanor drug charges against them were dismissed.</p><p>But their forfeiture case is still dragging on.</p><p>In early March, the officer involved failed to appear in court. That prompted a delay until late April.</p><p>The men — who said they couldn’t afford a lawyer because his fee would be more than what they're trying to get back — have now been waiting nearly a year.</p><p>“This thing just keeps dragging on with no end in sight,” says one, speaking on the condition of not being named.</p><h3><b>One man’s win</b></h3><p>Every once in a while, someone scores a victory.</p><p>Wynton Kyle Dozier, 40, got his 2014 Ford Fusion back on March 5 when prosecutors dropped his forfeiture case.</p><p>Chicago police officers had arrested Dozier the day after Christmas in 2024 after stopping him for failing to use a turn signal. Officers said they found drugs in the car.</p><p>In August, a judge threw out the criminal case, ruling the search was illegal.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A 2010 Ford Fusion Hybrid.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Dozier hired a lawyer to fight the criminal charges, but he handled the forfeiture case on his own. It took more than eight months to recover his car, which prosecutors valued at $4,150.</p><p>“They just want you to give up and take your things for free,” Dozier says.</p><p>He says he never understood why he had to fight two legal battles — one for his freedom and another for his car.</p><p>“It doesn’t make sense,” he says.</p><p>Another man, Maurice Walker, 63, decided to make a deal. His 2013 Cadillac, valued at $2,800, was seized in Markham after police in the suburb stopped him last April for running a red light. He was arrested for driving on a license suspended because of a DUI, a charge prosecutors dropped last July<b>.</b></p><p>Complicating his case, prosecutors had released his Cadillac CTS to a woman who said she needed the car, claiming a hardship.</p><p>At a recent forfeiture hearing, Walker was confused why he still needed to fight to get his car back.</p><p>“My case was dismissed,” he told the judge. “How do I owe you anything? The only thing left is them trying to take my car.”</p><p>A prosecutor responded: “The criminal case don’t mean nothing.”</p><p>The judge explained the legal differences between a criminal case and a civil forfeiture case.</p><p>After huddling with the prosecutor, Walker agreed to give the police $1,050 for fees for towing and storing his car.</p><p>The judge told Walker he wouldn’t have to go to trial to fight for his car as long as he pays up by May.</p><p>“I’m OK with that,” Walker replied. “Thank you, judge.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/02/20/dea-cash-forfeitures-trump-biden-gold-miner-civil-rights " target="_blank" >DEA didn’t arrest gold miner stopped at Union Station but seized his $115K and kept it for 7 years</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><h3><b>Millions to Chicago police</b></h3><p>How often property owners win or lose isn't clear. Those numbers aren't reported to the Illinois State Police.</p><p>The money involved is easier to trace. Under state law, proceeds from seized cash and auctioned property are distributed by the state police. The seizing agency gets 65%, the local state’s attorney’s office 12.5%, appellate prosecutors 12.5%, and the state police 10% for administering the program.</p><p>According to the latest report from the state police, reflecting 2024 seizures, the Chicago Police Department took in $9.4 million in assets that year — including 962 vehicles worth more than $7.7 million, plus cash. Every other law enforcement agency in Illinois combined reported seizing 595 vehicles.</p><p>A Chicago police spokesman says civil asset forfeiture "plays an important role in disrupting organized criminal networks," saying the money goes toward “strengthening public safety."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-570000" name="module-570000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>CHICAGO POLICE FORFEITURES</h3><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-78d3ea20-1e10-11f1-a08f-7df7c31be9ee" data-pm-slice="3 3 []"><li>In 2024, the Chicago Police Department collected $1.3 million from the Illinois State Police through the process of various agencies sharing the money from civil asset forfeitures.</li><li>The department spent $1.4 million, including $1.2 million for operating expenses, $77,000 for informants and undercover drug buys and $67,000 for travel, meals and training. </li><li>In recent years, the department also spent forfeiture funds on car leases, phone service, vehicle repairs, lab equipment — and hundreds of thousands of dollars that went to a company that supplies surveillance technology to law enforcement agencies, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, records show.</li><li>Those records also show that, in April 2025, roughly $4.5 million was sitting in the Chicago Police Department’s drug forfeiture fund along with $409,000 in a forfeiture fund tied to money-laundering seizures. That was nearly 40% less than the department held in 2020 — a drop sources say is tied to a sharp decline in search warrants following reforms prompted by wrongful police raids.</li></ul></div> </div><p>Under a law that took effect Jan. 1, the state police will collect even more information from police agencies, including the property owner's race, sex, age and ZIP code as well as more data about the spending of forfeiture money, including purchases of surveillance technology.</p><h3>A tool — or abuse?</h3><p>Despite the big money involved, Weitzel, the former Riverside police chief, rejects the idea that civil asset forfeiture is a money grab.</p><p>Forfeiture is “one of the few tools that weakens criminal networks financially, not just through arrests,” Weitzel says.</p><p>He says strict controls governed how his department seized and spent forfeiture funds.</p><p>But critics say the system needs changes. Some point to Michigan, where Gov. Gretchen Whitmer signed bipartisan legislation in 2019 largely banning police from forfeiting property worth $50,000 or less without a criminal conviction. Lawmakers later modified the law to allow forfeitures over $20,000 at airports without a conviction.</p><p>If that law applied in Illinois, lots of the civil asset forfeiture cases that now go through Courtroom 1707 would never be filed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-660000" name="image-660000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" sprawling Will County home, tossing flash-bang grenades as they stormed inside.<br><br>Their targets were Jeff Regnier and Greta Keranen, a couple accused of pocketing $275,000 through federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/ppp-paycheck-protection-program-covid-relief" target="_blank" >COVID-19 relief programs.</a> Officers also raided the home of Regnier’s father — a retired Chicago cop — though he never was charged with any crime.<br><br>The criminal case against Regnier and Keranen is still in court. But, in a dramatic twist, the couple has beaten a separate attempt by Will County prosecutors to seize millions of dollars in investment accounts and six vehicles under Illinois’ civil asset forfeiture laws.<br><br>Two of those vehicles — late-model Ford Broncos — prompted a blistering rebuke to prosecutors from a Will County judge who ordered the SUVs returned in January.<br><br>“The money-laundering statute is not a catchall for all things that the state cannot find in a legitimate way to seize,” Judge Brian Barrett wrote.<br><br>Barrett said he was “particularly disturbed with the special authoritarianism” displayed by the government.<br><br>Will County prosecutors are appealing.<br><br>The Regnier-Keranen saga spotlights the hotly debated civil asset forfeiture system, which allows police and prosecutors to seize property they believe is tied to crime — even if the owner is never convicted of any crime.<br><br>Civil rights advocates say the system flips the presumption of innocence on its head.<br><br>Not so, according to the Will County state’s attorney’s office, which says its prosecutors use “all legally available channels to fight crime and serve the residents of Will County,” noting that the Illinois General Assembly has deemed forfeiture “an important tool” and made reforms to the system in 2018.<br><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> It’s been tough.”<br><br>“They have made life very difficult for us,” Keranen said.<br><br>The couple eventually recovered $4.4 million from frozen investment accounts but say Will County still owes them about $2 million in lost investment gains.<br><br><h3>More legal fights ahead</h3><br>The original criminal case tied to the pandemic loans is now on hold as a judge considers a request from the couple to appoint a special prosecutor to investigate Will County’s forfeiture unit and federal agents.<br><br>In a court filing, the couple’s lawyer argues that the alleged abuses of the forfeiture system in the case were “neither isolated nor an aberration in Will County.”<br><br>Andreano said forfeiture laws allow government agencies to build “slush funds” with little oversight.<br><br>He also said prosecutors had a financial incentive in the couple’s case: Any restitution ordered in the criminal case would go to the federal Small Business Administration, not to Will County.<br><br>“So they filed a forfeiture case to grab money for the county,” he said.<br><br>Andreano is challenging Illinois forfeiture laws in another case, this one involving an 85-year-old woman whose 2014 Mazda CX-5 was seized by New Lenox police after her daughter was stopped for an expired registration sticker.<br><br>Regnier, who ran unsuccessfully for Congress in a Republican primary in 2022, said the forfeiture system gives prosecutors enormous leverage.<br><br>“They hold you under water and say, ‘Let’s make a deal,’ ” he said.<br><br>Keranen said she witnessed the human toll of the system while in court.<br><br>“We saw people coming into the forfeiture court crying,” she said. “I think it needs reform. I’m not sure it needs to be abolished. But they shouldn’t be able to take your stuff without proving a crime.”</div> </div><p></p>
